text.p: Ford Motor Co said Thursday it will again restructure its global product development operations, reducing the number of vehicle centers to three from five.

The changes, which also call for Ford to have 11 vehicle line directors, come less than two years after the automaker embarked on its ambitious "Ford 2000" global reorganization plan, which combined U.S. and European development groups into a single unit.

Following a board of directors meeting Thursday, Ford said it named Jim Englehart as group vice president in charge of product development, succeeding Jacques Nasser, who was elected president of Ford Automotive Operations.
Englehart was previously vice president for the vehicle center that developed light trucks primarily for personal use.

Going forward, Ford will have three vehicle centers for car and truck development -- Truck, to be headed by vice president Jim Donaldson; Small and Medium Car, to be headed by vice president Richard Parry-Jones; and Large and Luxury Car, to be headed by vice president Ken Kohrs.
The small and medium-car development center will continue to be based in Merkenich, Germany, and Dunton, England, while both the truck and large/luxury car centers will be based in Dearborn, Mich.

Previously, Ford had a development center in Merkenich and Dunton for small front-drive cars and Dearborn-based centers for large front-drive cars, for rear-drive cars, for light trucks and for commercial trucks.
Ford's staff of vehicle line directors -- each of whom will be responsible for a major family of vehicle models -- has been reduced to 11 from 17 previously.
"We have beeen able to simplify and streamline the organizational structure now that we are reducing our vehicle platforms by 50 percent," Ford Chairman Alex Trotman said in a statement.

"Using the 16 vehicle plaforms and at the same time increasing the number of derivatives, we can provide a broader array of vehicles for customers in many more markets," Trotman said. "This simplified product system will help us intensify efforts to improve quality and lower costs."

A Ford spokesman said the reorganization will not result in any new employment reduction initiatives beyond the early retirement programs and efforts to reduce contract positions that were previously in place.
